::: {.center}
# 1 Pretraining {data-name="Pretraining"}
:::

## 1.1 Pretrain once, reuse many times

| Stage | Data | Labels | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Pretraining** | billions of letters of genome sequence | none | Mistral-DNA: the human genome |
| **Adaptation** | one task's data set | thousands | AGO2: 92,000 labelled sequences |

- **Claim**: what a model learns in pretraining transfers, so each task needs fewer labels
- Slots 5 to 7 test that claim on AGO2

::: {.notes}
Presenter: Roee.

- Most models so far, like our CNN, are trained from random weights for one task with that task's labels.
- A foundation model is first trained on genome sequence alone. Each task then adds a small output layer (a head) and may adjust the model.
- Heads differ by task: a number (expression level), a label per position (splice sites), or one probability per sequence, as today.
:::

## 1.2 Each model cuts DNA into different tokens

![](assets/custom/tokens.png){fig-align="center" height="659px"}

::: {.notes}
- Real tokenizers on a real bound sequence, in DNA letters (the models were trained on DNA, so U becomes T).
- Mistral-DNA and DNABERT-2 use the same learned vocabulary, built by byte-pair encoding (BPE): frequent substrings become single tokens, so token lengths vary.
- Nucleotide Transformer uses fixed 6-letter tokens. Shifting the sequence by one letter changes every token (bottom row); the remainder becomes single letters.
- The underlined miR-19 site is split differently by each tokenizer. No model sees it as one unit.
:::

## 1.3 From tokens to an embedding

- **Embedding**: the last layer's output, averaged over all non-padding tokens (including the special tokens `[CLS]` and `[SEP]`)
- **Linear probe**: a logistic regression trained on embeddings, with the model frozen

![](assets/custom/pipeline_real.png){fig-align="center" height="538px"}

::: {.notes}
- Mistral-DNA on the first 60 letters of one real sequence: each token is mapped to an integer, the model outputs one 256-number vector per token in its last layer, and we average those vectors.
- In a batch, shorter sequences are padded. The attention mask (1 for real tokens, 0 for padding) keeps padding out of the average.
- A few dimensions are large for almost every token (the vertical stripes). That is common in transformer models and does not depend on the sequence.
- Before the logistic regression each of the 256 dimensions is standardised.
- We do not open the model's internals (attention) today. For our purposes it is a function from tokens to vectors.
:::

## 1.4 Two pretraining objectives

- **Next token** (Mistral-DNA, HyenaDNA, Evo): $\;\mathcal{L} = -\log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$
- **Masked tokens** (Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2): $\;\mathcal{L} = -\log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{\setminus t})$, hidden tokens predicted from both sides

![](assets/custom/next_token.png){fig-align="center" height="492px"}

::: {.notes}
- The figure: Mistral-DNA, given the first tokens of a real sequence, assigns a probability to each of its 4,096 possible next tokens. Its top choice gets about 10%; the true token is shown at the bottom with its much lower probability.
- Much of the genome is hard to predict from local context, so the loss stays high even in a trained model.
- Masked models hide about 15% of the tokens and predict them from the tokens on both sides.
- In both cases the genome supplies its own targets, so no experimental labels are needed.
:::

## 1.5 The landscape, 2021 to 2025

![](assets/custom/landscape.png){fig-align="center" height="700px"}

::: {.notes}
- DNABERT (110M parameters), Nucleotide Transformer (50M to 2.5B), DNABERT-2 and HyenaDNA, then Evo (7B) and Evo 2 (40B).
- Filled points are masked models, open points next-token models.
- Not shown: Enformer, Borzoi and AlphaGenome, trained with labels from thousands of experiments; currently the strongest models for gene regulation.
- Slot 8 shows ten models from these families tested on AGO2.
:::

::: {.center}
# 2 Adapting {data-name="Adapting"}
:::

## 2.1 Four ways to adapt a pretrained model

| Method | Trained | Cost |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Linear probe | a new output layer only (after one pass to compute embeddings) | seconds to minutes |
| Partial fine-tuning | the output layer and the top layers | minutes |
| Full fine-tuning | all weights | hours |
| LoRA | small low-rank matrices added to each layer | minutes |

::: {.notes}
- "Fine-tuning" usually refers to the last three; the first is called probing. Slot 5 uses a probe, Slot 7 uses LoRA.
- Full fine-tuning with few labels overfits easily.
:::

## 2.2 LoRA

$$W x \;\rightarrow\; (W + BA)\,x, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times 256},\; r = 16$$

![](assets/custom/lora.png){fig-align="center" height="605px"}

::: {.notes}
- LoRA keeps each large weight matrix W fixed and learns a low-rank correction BA. Here W is one real 256 × 256 matrix from Mistral-DNA: 65,536 frozen weights against 8,192 trained ones.
- B starts at zero, so training begins exactly from the pretrained model.
- Across the models in our tests, LoRA trained between about 1% and 9% of the parameters.
- A 16M-parameter model could be fully fine-tuned on a laptop GPU; LoRA is how 500M-parameter models are adapted on modest hardware. Slot 7 uses it on Mistral-DNA so the students practise the method.

Next: Slot 5, where the students load a pretrained model and probe it.
:::
